titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §241–257: oxen, hired men and the farm-steward (xxxvi 81 – xxxviii 4)
part: Laws §241–257 · oxen, hired men & the farm-steward (Col. xxxvi 81 – xxxviii 4)
about: Seventeen laws on hired animals and hired men. The first block is about oxen that are hired or seized: an ox seized as a pledge costs a third of a mina (§241); two kinds of hired ox or team, whose Sumerian names I cannot read, cost four and three kor of grain a year (§242–243). Then who bears the loss of a hired animal: its owner, if a lion kills it in the open country (§244); the hirer, who must replace the ox with an ox like it if he kills it through carelessness or a beating or breaks its foot (§245–246), half its price for its eye and a quarter for its horns, tail or flesh (§247–248); but not if a god strikes it, when his oath frees him (§249). Next the goring ox (§250–252): no claim if it gores a man as it goes along; but if it was known as a gorer, its owner was told and did nothing, and it kills a man’s son, he pays half a mina, and a third of a mina for a slave. The last block is the hired farm-steward (§253–256), put in charge of a field with supplies and cattle: if he is caught stealing seed or fodder his hands are cut off; if he weakens the cattle he makes up the grain; if he hires the cattle out or grows no crop he measures out sixty kor for every ten bur; and if he cannot pay he is dragged about the field with the cattle. The part ends with a hired man’s wage, eight kor of grain a year (§257). Several words are not readable from the grammar and I say so in the notes: the two named oxen (§242–243), labiānu and pasuttu (parts of the ox), aldāʾam, tâna, pīḫatu, the hired man’s title AK.ŠU, and some verbs (ittasak, ušarrim, imtanaššarūšu). Col. XXXVI ends at line 91 and col. XXXVII runs to line 101; Harper’s line numerals agree with his own section headings throughout.

sentences.i: If a man has distrained an ox as a hostage (a pledge for debt),
sentences.n: Here the laws on hired and seized animals and on hired men begin (§241–257: oxen §241–252, the hired field-steward §253–256, a hired man §257). The usual šumma pattern: šumma awīlum … “if a man …”, the condition in the perfect, the penalty in the present. alpam is the one sign GU₄ “ox”, with no -am written (on the plate the same word is sometimes GU₄ alone and sometimes GU₄ + the sign AM; I note which each time). ana nibūtim ittebi: ittebi is the perfect of nebûm “to distrain, seize as a pledge” and nibūtim “as a hostage (for debt)”; both words are as in §114–116, where a person is the pledge; here it is an ox. The sense “seize an ox for a debt” is Harper’s; it is what the penalty in the next line fits.

sentences.i: he shall pay one third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: The penalty for a wrongful distraint: ⅓ mana kaspim išaqqal. ⅓ is one sign (the fraction “one third”), said šalšāt, a reconstructed spoken form (?); ma-na is two syllables, mana “mina”; kaspim is the logogram KÙ.BABBAR “silver”, written with the two signs KÙ and BABBAR and no ending (Harper’s kaspim is his normalization, as in the earlier parts); išaqqal is the present of šaqālum “to weigh (out)”, the verb for paying silver (“he shall pay”). As in the whole code, the penalty is in the present tense and means “he shall”.

sentences.i: If a man has hired (an animal?) for one year,
sentences.n: agārum “to hire”: īgur “he hired” (no -ma is written; the next unit gives the hire as a sentence of its own). The thing hired is not named in these lines; the next lines name it by its hire, and §243 says the hire goes “to its owner”, so what is hired has an owner. šattim “year” is written with the year-sign MU alone and no ending (Harper prints šattim; on the plate MU is followed straight away by one vertical wedge, the numeral 1, and then i-gur); 1 is said ištēt because šattum is feminine (a reconstructed spoken form, (?)). ana šattim ištēt “for one year”.

sentences.i: the hire of a GU₄.DA.UR.RA (a kind of hired ox or team?; unread) is four kor of grain.
sentences.n: A sentence with no verb: the hire (ID = Á, the arm sign, “hire”, idum; the case ending is not written) of GU₄.DA.UR.RA is 4 kor of grain. Harper writes ID; the plate sign is the sign Á (A₂), as in §224. GU₄.DA.UR.RA is a Sumerian-looking compound of four signs after Á that I cannot read (Harper’s List of Signs, no. 109, gives it as GUD.DA.UR.RA); GU₄ “ox” opens it, and the context (a hire for a year, §243 with a lower hire) says it is a named kind of working ox or ox-team. I leave it unread and UNCERTAIN; the plate row has exactly the five sign-groups of Harper’s ID GUD.DA.UR.RA. IV is the numeral 4, said erbet (?) before a masculine noun; ŠE.GUR is “kor of grain” (a grain measure of about 300 qa, as in §44 ff.).

sentences.l: the-hire of-GU₄.LID.UD.SAG three kor-of-grain to its-owner he-shall-give.
sentences.i: the hire of a GU₄.LID.UD.SAG (another kind of hired ox?; unread) is three kor of grain; he shall give it to its owner.
sentences.n: The second named hire: Á “hire” + the compound GU₄.LID.UD.SAG (GU₄ “ox”, LID “cow”, UD “day / sun”, SAG “head”), which I cannot read; UNCERTAIN, and I do not guess what the signs mean together. Harper’s transliteration prints GU₄.UD.LID.SAG, but on the plate the diamond (LID) stands second and the UD sign third, and his own List of Signs (no. 109) writes GU₄.LID.UD.SAG, so I follow the plate. The hire is three kor, one less than §242, so this is the lesser (or different) animal. ana bēlišu inaddin “to its owner he shall give”: the verb stands at the end of §243; whether it is meant for §242 as well is not marked. bēlišu is bēlum “owner” with -šu “his/its”; inaddin is the present of nadānum “to give”. III is the numeral 3, said šalāšat (?) before a masculine noun.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox a-donkey he-has-hired-and, in-the-open-country a-lion has-killed-him,
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox or a donkey, and a lion has killed it in the open country,
sentences.n: Two animals are listed without “or”: alpam imēram īgurma “has hired an ox, a donkey, and”. ina ṣērim “in the open country” (the steppe, as in §17). UR.MAḪ is the two signs UR “dog” + MAḪ “great” and means “lion”; I write nēšum, but labbum is also “lion” and the signs do not choose (Harper prints MAH with a plain H). iddūkšu (id-du-uk-šu) is read as “has killed him/it”: the perfect of dâkum “to kill” with -šu “him/it”, the doubled d being the perfect’s infix -ta- assimilated to the root’s d, the middle ʾ contracted to ū (the perfect is the tense of the protasis throughout the code; elsewhere Harper writes i-du-uk, as in idukkū, for the present); UNCERTAIN in form, as the stem vowels are only read from the shape. Here alpam is GU₄ + AM and imēram is ANŠE alone (the sign for “donkey”).

sentences.i: the loss is for its owner alone.
sentences.n: ana bēlišuma: “to its owner only” — the verb is not written; the sense is that the loss falls on the owner (the lender), not on the man who hired the animal. -ma here is not the clause-chaining “and” but the emphatic “only, alone”, as in ša aḫḫīšama (§180). “The loss” is supplied in the English.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox he-has-hired-and, through-carelessness or through-beating he-has-caused-to-die,
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox and has killed it through carelessness or through a beating,
sentences.n: ina mēgūtim “through carelessness”: mēgūtum is read from the signs me-gu-tim (negligence, Harper’s sense; UNCERTAIN as a word, the sense is the one the law needs). ù lu is written as two words, ù “and” + lu “or”, which together mean “or” (as in earlier parts): ù lu ina maḫāṣim “or through beating” (maḫāṣum “to strike”; the ṣi is written with the sign ZI, which Harper prints zi; the line has a second tier, where the word breaks after ḫa). uštamīt is the Š-stem perfect of mâtum “to die”: “has caused to die” (§219 ff.). Line 7 has alpam as GU₄ alone, no -am.

sentences.i: he shall replace the ox for its owner with an ox like it.
sentences.n: alpam kīma alpim “an ox like the ox” (kīma “like, as” + genitive); ana bēl alpim “to the owner of the ox” (bēl is the construct, “owner of”); iriab “he shall replace” (riābum, as in §53–54). The order is the Akkadian one: the thing replaced first, the person after. The first alpam here is GU₄ + the sign AM (the second sign is the ornate AM), the second alpim is GU₄ alone.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox he-has-hired-and, its-feet he-has-broken or its-labiānu he-has-cut,
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox and has broken its foot (or feet), or has cut its labiānu (?),
sentences.n: The injury laws start (§246–248): a hired ox is hurt. šêpi-šu is Harper’s normalization of a logogram: one sign NER (the sign of “foot”, šēpum: his List of Signs no. 170, “ner, kiš, šēpu”) + šu, “its feet”; the ending -ī- is a plural or dual, but the sign gives no number, so one foot or both is UNCERTAIN. ištebir is the perfect of šebērum “to break”. labiānšu (la-bi-a-an-šu) is a word I cannot read: a part of the ox (Harper treats it as a body part); UNCERTAIN, it is left untranslated. ittakis is the perfect of nakāsum “to cut”. Line 15 has alpam as GU₄ alone.

sentences.i: he shall replace the ox for its owner with an ox like it.
sentences.n: The same penalty as §245: a hurt foot or labiānu costs a whole ox, not a part of its price. Line 19 has alpam as GU₄ + AM and alpim as GU₄ alone.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox he-has-hired-and, its-eye he-has-destroyed,
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox and has destroyed its eye,
sentences.n: īnšu “its eye”: Harper’s în-šu is the logogram IGI (īnum, “eye”) + šu. uḫtabbit is the perfect of the D-stem of ḫabātum, which I take (as in §196) as “has destroyed”, from the sense of the law, not from the verb: UNCERTAIN. The last sign is the DA sign where uḫ-tab-bi-it needs the sign IT: Harper prints uḫ-tab-da(=it) and marks it a carver’s slip.

sentences.l: silver half of-its-price to the-owner-of-the-ox he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall give the owner of the ox silver, half of its price.
sentences.n: kaspi mišil šīmišu “silver, half of its price”: kaspum is the logogram KÙ.BABBAR (Harper prints kaspi; the plate shows only the two signs KÙ and BABBAR, no complement, so I write none); mišil “half” is mi-ši-il; šīmišu is ŠÁM “price” + šu, “its price”. Half the price for a lost eye, a whole ox for a broken foot (§246): the code grades the loss. The penalty is paid to the owner (ana bēl alpim) with the usual inaddin.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox he-has-hired-and, its-horns he-has-broken, its-tail he-has-cut, or the-flesh of-its-pasuttu he-has-thrown(?),
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox and has broken its horns, cut off its tail, or torn off (?) the flesh of its pasuttu (?),
sentences.n: Three injuries in a row: išbir “has broken” (preterite of šebērum) with qarnīšu “its horns” (the form is oblique, a plural or dual, so “horns”); ittakis “has cut” with zibbassu “its tail” (Harper’s zibba-zu: the logogram ZIB, zibbatum “tail”, + the sign ZU standing for -ssu, as in nibūssu); then ulu šīr pasuttišu ittasak. šīr is the logogram SU “flesh” (šīrum; Harper’s sign no. 80, šēru). pasuttum is written with two signs, not syllabically: Harper’s List of Signs (no. 50) gives it as the corner sign SA plus a second sign and calls it pasuttu, a part of the ox that I cannot read. The second sign (a triangle with a small diamond in it and a long tail wedge) I could not identify; it is keyed UL only as the nearest shape. On the plate row (XXXVII 32) the triangle sign stands before the corner sign, between SU and šu, where Harper’s List prints SA first; the glyphs follow the plate, so the reading is X.SA (X = the unidentified sign), and the order is UNCERTAIN along with the whole word. ittasak (it-ta-sa-ak) is the perfect of nasākum “to throw, cast”; “tear off” is a guess from the sense, UNCERTAIN: the sign AK could also be aq, nasāqum “to pick out”. Line 29 has alpam as GU₄ alone.

sentences.i: he shall give silver, a quarter of its price.
sentences.n: IGI.IV.GAL is the logogram for “a quarter” (rebūt, as in §225): IGI, 4, GAL. A quarter of the price for the horns, the tail or the flesh; half for the eye (§247). The recipient (the owner) is understood from the earlier laws; here there is no ana bēl alpim.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox he-has-hired-and, a-god has-struck-him-and he-has-died,
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox and a god has struck it and it has died,
sentences.n: ilum imḫassuma imtūt: ilum is “a god” (the animal is “struck by a god”: a death with no human cause); imḫassuma is imḫaṣ “struck” (maḫāṣum) + -šu “him” (the sign ZU stands for -ssu, as in amḫassu §206) + -ma “and”; imtūt is the perfect of mâtum “to die”. Line 37 has alpam as GU₄ alone.

sentences.l: the-man who the-ox hired, the-oath of-the-god he-shall-declare-and he-shall-be-released.
sentences.i: the man who hired the ox shall swear the oath of the god and go free.
sentences.n: awīlum ša alpam īguru “the man who hired the ox” (ša “who, which”, īguru with the relative -u). nīš ilim izakkarma “he shall swear the oath of the god, and” (as in §103), ūtaššar “he shall be released” (the Dt of wašārum, as in §103). The oath is the hirer’s proof that the ox died by a god’s act and not through his fault; the loss falls on the owner (§244). I take alpam here as GU₄ alone (the line has a second tier and is crowded).

sentences.l: If an-ox the-street(?) in-its-going a-man has-gored-and has-caused-to-die,
sentences.i: If an ox, going along the street (?), has gored a man and killed him,
sentences.n: The goring-ox laws (§250–252). alpum here is GU₄ + um (the subject of the clause). zu-ga-am (Harper’s zugam) is a word I cannot place with confidence. What the grammar allows: an accusative ending -am, followed by ina alākišu “in its going”, so a word for a place or way the ox went along. If zu stands for su (z for s is not rare in Old Babylonian spelling) and ga for qa₂, the word is sūqam “street”, an accusative of the way gone (alākum with a road for its object): “as it goes along the street”. UNCERTAIN: the spelling with z is not confirmed, and the rendering rests on this. Other words of the shape zuq- (a form of zuqtum, “peak”) would show a t, which is not written here. ina alākišu “in its going” (alākum “to go”, the infinitive with -šu). ikkipma: Harper prints ik-ki-ib-ma, but the sign IB also has the value ip (his List of Signs no. 186, “ib, ip”) and the verb is nakāpum “to gore, butt” (as in munakkip, “gorer of”), so I say ikkipma (preterite + -ma), “has gored, and”; the reading with b is Harper’s. uštamīt is the Š-stem of mâtum, “has caused to die”.

sentences.i: that case has no claim.
sentences.n: dīnum šū rugummâm ul īšu: “that case has no claim” (as in §115, §123): the owner of the ox has no right of action against anyone for a death that happened this way. īšu is the verb išûm “to have”, the plain form “he has” (no subjunctive ending is involved; the subjunctive would be īšû).

sentences.i: If a man’s ox is a gorer,
sentences.n: alap awīlim “the ox of a man” (alap is the construct of alpum, “ox of”). nakkāpum, “gorer, butting (ox)”, is read from na-ak-ka-…: the noun of the verb nakāpum “to gore”. Harper’s square brackets (a[m-ma]) mean the last signs are restored, and the sign before them is written A, not PU (as in the next line, na-ak-ka-pu-u), so the exact form (nakkāpam-ma, or a predicate nakkāpma) is UNCERTAIN; the sense “is a gorer” is not. Here alap is GU₄ alone.

sentences.i: and its defect (?) as a gorer has been made known to him,
sentences.n: kīma nakkapû “as a gorer” (UNCERTAIN: the ending -û is Harper’s; the spelling is na-ak-ka-pu-u). babtašu “its babtum”: babtum is the word of §126 (see the glossary), where it is read as the party held answerable; here Harper’s “loss, defects” suits the ox, “its defect”, and I use that; UNCERTAIN, and the other reading (his babtum, his ward or neighbours, as the subject) would make the same sentence “his ward has made it known to him”. ušēdišumma: the Š preterite of edûm (ušēdi “he made known”) + -šum “to him” + -ma “and”; no subject is named, so I write it as a passive. The law is built on notice: the owner has been told the ox gores. The line has a second tier where the word breaks after ka.

sentences.l: its-horns not he-has-trimmed(?), his-ox not he-has-checked(?)-and,
sentences.i: and he has not trimmed (?) its horns and has not kept his ox in check (?),
sentences.n: Two things the owner failed to do: qarnīšu lā ušarrim, “he has not (ušarrim?) its horns”, and alpīšu lā usanniqma, “he has not (sanāqum) his ox, and”. ušarrim (u-šar-ri-im) looks like a D-stem preterite (u-šarrim) of a verb whose root I cannot fix; the sense “cut back, trim (the horns)” is what the context needs, and nothing else supports it: UNCERTAIN. usanniq is read as the D-stem of sanāqum, taken as “to keep in check”; UNCERTAIN, the sense is from the context alone. Both verbs are preterites after lā, “has not”. alpīšu is GU₄ + šu, “his ox”. The line has a second tier, breaking after sa.

sentences.i: and that ox has gored a man’s son and killed him,
sentences.n: alpum šū “that ox” (here GU₄ + um); mār awīlim “a man’s son” (DUMU, with no ending: the son of a free man, as in §196 ff.); ikkipma (Harper: ikkibma, see §250) and uštamīt as there. The condition of §251 ends here: a known gorer, a warning given, nothing done, and a freeborn man’s son is killed.

sentences.i: he shall give half a mina of silver.
sentences.n: ½ is one sign (the fraction “one half”), said mišil; Harper restores ma in [ma]-na and na in i-[na]-ad-di-in, the two broken syllables (UNCERTAIN as signs; the words are secure). The payment for a freeborn son’s death is half a mina of silver; no one is named to receive it.

sentences.l: If a-man’s slave, a-third of-a-mina of-silver he-shall-give.
sentences.i: If it is a man’s slave, he shall give one third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: A short law that finishes the previous clause: “if (the ox has gored) a man’s slave, he shall give ⅓ mana of silver”. warad awīlim is ARAD (no ending written) + awīlim; kaspim is KÙ.BABBAR with no ending, as above, “a man’s slave”. Harper’s square brackets mark šum-ma as restored (the first signs of the line are lost; UNCERTAIN as signs, not as sense). “The ox has gored” is understood.

sentences.l: If a-man a-man to the-front of-his-field to-stand he-has-hired-and,
sentences.i: If a man has hired a man to take charge of his field,
sentences.n: The farm-steward laws (§253–256): a man hires another to “stand at the front of his field”, ana pāni eqlišu uzuzzim, that is, to be in charge of it (uzuzzum, the infinitive of izuzzum “to stand”, written u-zu-uz-zi-im; literally “to stand before his field”, which I take as “to attend to it, be in charge of it”: a reading from the sense, UNCERTAIN). eqlišu is A.ŠÀ + šu, “his field”. Line 69 has a second tier (awīlam, the hired man). The steward is never named; I call him the hired man or the steward.

sentences.i: and has entrusted the aldāʾam (?) to him,
sentences.n: aldāʾam (Harper’s al-dá-a-am) is a word I cannot read; the context (§254, where the steward “takes” it, and §253 below, “seed or fodder”) points to farm supplies, such as seed-grain, but that is a guess: UNCERTAIN, left as aldāʾam. iqīpšu “he has entrusted to him” is the preterite (iqīp) of qiāpum (as in §107) + -šu: Harper’s [i]-qi-ip-šu, with the first sign restored (in square brackets), the KI sign read qi, the IB sign read ip.

sentences.i: has put the cattle in his charge, and has bound him to cultivate the field,
sentences.n: LID.GUD.ZUN is the Sumerogram for “cattle” (liātum, as in §35: the cow, ox and plural signs; the first sign is damaged on the plate, drawn in outline, and Harper restores it in square brackets). ip-ki-zum is read ipqissum, “he has entrusted to him”, from paqādum “to entrust, care for” + -šum, the ss from d + š (Harper prints ki, the KI sign here read qi, and the sign ZUM for ssum, as in ūlissum §167). ana eqlim erēšim “to cultivate the field” (erēšum “to cultivate”; eqlim written A.ŠÀ + lim). urakkissu: the D-stem of rakāsum “to bind, bind by a contract” + -šu, “he has bound him (to it)”, with the last sign su (Harper prints it with a small mark; it is SU, not ŠU: UNCERTAIN). Harper restores [a-na], the first words of the line. The man’s duties are now fixed: the field, the supplies, the cattle, and the contract.

sentences.l: If that man seed-grain or ŠÀ.GAL has-stolen-and, in-his-hand has-been-seized,
sentences.i: If that man has stolen seed-grain or fodder (?) and is caught with it in his hand,
sentences.n: The theft clause of the steward’s contract (a second šumma inside §253). šū “that” (awīlum šū “that man”, the hired steward). ŠE.ZIR is the logogram “seed-grain” (ŠE “grain” + ZIR, Harper’s sign for zērum “seed”); ŠÀ.GAL is a Sumerogram I cannot read, two signs (ŠÀ “heart, inside”, GAL “big”); “fodder” is what the pairing with seed and the cattle suggest: UNCERTAIN. išriqma: išriq “he stole” (šarāqum) + -ma. ina qātišu: “in his hand”; Harper prints ga-ti-šu, the GA sign here read qa (qa₂). ittaṣbat is the N-stem perfect of ṣabātum “to seize”, “has been seized, caught” (as in §19, §132).

sentences.i: they shall cut off his hands.
sentences.n: The penalty: rittēšu inakkisū, “his hands they shall cut off” (the same phrase as §195 ff.: UM.ME-šu, the two signs read as “hands” by Harper’s list; the number, “hands” or “hand”, is UNCERTAIN). inakkisū is the present plural of nakāsum “to cut”: the sentence is unspecific (“they”), as often in the code.

sentences.i: If he has taken the aldāʾam (?) and has weakened the cattle,
sentences.n: Misuse of what he was entrusted with. aldāʾam as in §253 (UNCERTAIN word). ilqēma: ilqe “he took” (leqûm) + -ma. utenniš “he has weakened”: the D-stem preterite of enēšum (a D perfect would be uttenniš) “to be weak” (the adjective enšum “weak” is in the prologue); the cattle are over-worked or starved. The condition continues in the next unit, where the steward must make good the loss.

sentences.i: he shall replace the tâna (?) of grain that they hoed (?).
sentences.n: tâna (Harper’s ta-a-na) is a word I cannot read; it names something measured in grain, “the (loss, yield, amount) of grain”: UNCERTAIN, left as tâna. ša imrirū: imrirū (the plural ending -ū is also the subjunctive ending after ša) is read as a preterite plural of marārum “to hoe, break up clods” (as in §44: imarrar “he shall hoe”), “which they hoed”; UNCERTAIN: the vowel i is not what a preterite beside imarrar would give (imrurū), so the root is in doubt too, and the subject (the cattle? his labourers?) is not stated. ŠE-im is the logogram ŠE + -im, “of grain” (šeʾim). iriab “he shall replace” (riābum). The sense: he must replace the grain lost through his abuse of the cattle (§254), but the two key words are unread and the English is only the sense.

sentences.l: If the-cattle of-a-man for-hire he-has-given, or seed-grain he-has-stolen-and, in-the-field not he-has-produced,
sentences.i: If he has hired out a man’s cattle, or has stolen seed-grain and has grown nothing in the field,
sentences.n: Two further offences by the steward: hiring out the owner’s cattle (ana igrim ittadin “he has hired out for hire”: ittadin is the perfect of nadānum, “has given (out)”, as in §34), or stealing the seed and producing no crop. ina eqlim lā uštabši “in the field he has not produced”: uštabši is the Š-stem perfect of bašûm “to exist”, “to bring into being, to grow (a crop)” (as in §42, §49). The steward is the subject throughout. “Has grown nothing” is the sense of lā uštabši with no object.

sentences.l: that man they-shall-convict-and, at-harvest ten bur sixty kor-of-grain he-shall-measure-out.
sentences.i: they shall convict that man, and at harvest he shall measure out sixty kor of grain (for) every ten bur.
sentences.n: awīlam šuāti “that man” (accusative); ukannūšuma “they shall convict him, and” (the D-stem of kânum, as in §42, §112). ina ebūrim X GAN.E LX ŠE.GUR imaddad: “at harvest, 10 bur, 60 kor of grain, he shall measure out”. The relation between the area and the grain is not written (no “for each”); I supply it because that is the only sense (a fixed yield: six kor to the bur). ebūrim is the one logogram BURU₁₄ “harvest” (Harper writes ebûrim); GAN.E is “bur” (būrum, the field measure of §44 ff.); X is 10 (said ešret), LX is 60 (šūši, “sixty”: the sexagesimal one), ŠE.GUR is “kor of grain”.

sentences.i: If he is not able to pay what he owes (?),
sentences.n: bi-ḫa-zu is Harper’s word and I cannot read it from the grammar: I read pīḫassu (pīḫatum + -šu, “his pīḫatu”), taking it as the obligation he owes under §255 (the grain); UNCERTAIN, from the context only. apālam is the infinitive of apālum “to pay”; lā ileʾʾi “he is not able” (leʾûm, as in §29: Harper prints i-li-i, the sign I twice). “To pay what he owes” rests on the guess for the first word.

sentences.i: they shall drag him about (?) in that field with the cattle.
sentences.n: ina eqlim šuāti “in that field”; ina LID.GUD.ZUN “with (or by) the cattle”: Harper prints GUD.LID.ZUN, but the plate shows the usual order LID, GUD, ZUN; I key the usual order. imtanaššarūšu is a Gtn present plural (the -tan- stem, “repeatedly”) of a verb mašārum + -šu “him”; I read it as “drag (about)”, which is Harper’s sense and what the Gtn and “with the cattle” suit; the root is UNCERTAIN, and so is the translation. The sense is a degrading punishment in the very field he failed to make yield. Line 99 has a second tier.

sentences.i: If a man has hired an AK.ŠU (a hired man, whose title I cannot read),
sentences.n: The last law of this part: a hired man’s yearly wage. AK.ŠU is two Sumerian-looking signs (AK, ŠU) that I cannot read as an Akkadian word (Harper lists it under AK, his sign no. 48); the context (hired for a year, paid in grain) says a hired worker of some kind: UNCERTAIN. īgur “he hired” (agārum, no -ma here). The unit crosses from col. XXXVII line 101 into col. XXXVIII line 1 (the stele line numbers start again at 1 in the new column).

sentences.i: he shall give him eight kor of grain a year.
sentences.n: The wage: VIII (eight, the numeral, said samānat (?)) ŠE.GUR “kor of grain”, ina šattim ištēt “in one year”, inaddiššum “he shall give him” (inaddin + -šum, the n of -in assimilated to the š: inaddiš-šum, as in §17, §191). šattim is MU alone, as in §242 (the plate shows MU, then the numeral 1, then KAM); 1{kam} is the numeral 1 with the sign KAM, said ištēt (?). Harper’s col. XXXVIII goes on with §258; the next part takes it up.
